sections.h2: What law governs a transfer on death deed in New Mexico?
sections.html:
New Mexico transfer on death deeds are governed by the Uniform Real Property Transfer on Death Act, found at 45-6-401 and following in the Uniform Probate Code. Section 45-6-405 NMSA 1978 states the basic rule in one sentence: an individual may transfer property to one or more beneficiaries, effective at the transferor's death, by a transfer on death deed.

The act took effect on January 1, 2014. Under 45-6-403 it applies to a transfer on death deed made before, on or after that date, as long as the transferor dies on or after January 1, 2014. The New Mexico Courts self-help guide, quoted elsewhere on this page, says these deeds have been available since June 2001. The statute and the court guide describe two different dates, and we point to the statute for the rules that apply today.

Section 45-6-404 adds that the act does not displace any other lawful way of passing property in New Mexico. A will, joint tenancy and a trust all remain available, and a transfer on death deed is one tool among them.

sections.h2: What must a New Mexico transfer on death deed contain?
sections.html:
The deed must look like an ordinary recordable deed, say that the transfer happens at death, and be recorded before the owner dies. Section 45-6-409 lists three requirements:

  • It contains the essential elements and formalities of a properly recordable inter vivos deed.
  • It states that the transfer to the designated beneficiary is to occur at the transferor's death.
  • It is recorded before the transferor's death in the office of the county clerk for the county where the property is located.

The recording step is the one people miss. A signed deed in a desk drawer does nothing. Because the deed has to be recorded with the clerk, the recording fee in 14-8-15 NMSA 1978 applies. That section sets the fee at $25 for each document recorded, with extra charges for large documents with many index entries.

Section 45-6-410 removes several steps that people expect. The deed does not require notice to the beneficiary, delivery to the beneficiary, acceptance by the beneficiary during the owner's life, or consideration. The owner can sign and record without telling the person named.

sections.h2: What can the owner still do after recording the deed?
sections.html:
Almost everything. During the owner's life, 45-6-412 says a transfer on death deed does not affect any interest or right of the transferor, including the right to transfer or encumber the property. An owner who has recorded one can still sell the house, refinance it or take out a loan against it.

The same section lists what the deed does not do while the owner is alive:

  • It does not affect the rights of a buyer, even one who knows about the deed.
  • It does not affect the rights of secured or unsecured creditors, current or future.
  • It does not affect the owner's or the beneficiary's eligibility for any form of public assistance.
  • It does not give the beneficiary a legal or equitable interest.
  • It does not expose the property to claims of the beneficiary's creditors.

For a homeowner who wants to sell, this is the key point. The beneficiary named in the deed cannot block a sale, and a buyer does not need the beneficiary's signature. The deed only takes effect if the owner still holds the property at death.

sections.h2: How can a transfer on death deed be changed or revoked?
sections.html:
Only by a new recorded instrument. Under 45-6-411, a revocation works only if it is acknowledged by the transferor after the acknowledgment of the deed being revoked, and recorded before the transferor's death in the county clerk's office where the deed is recorded. It must also take one of three forms: a new transfer on death deed that revokes the earlier one expressly or by inconsistency, an instrument that expressly revokes it, or a regular deed that expressly revokes it.

Two further rules prevent shortcuts. After a transfer on death deed is recorded, it cannot be revoked by a revocatory act on the deed itself, so tearing up a copy or writing across it does nothing. And if the deed was made by more than one owner, a revocation by one does not affect the others, while a deed of joint owners is revoked only if all living joint owners revoke it.

The New Mexico Courts self-help guide says the owner can revoke or amend without the beneficiary's consent or knowledge. That matches the statute, with the recording condition above.

sections.h2: What happens at the owner's death, and who gets the house?
sections.html:
If the named beneficiary survives the owner, the property passes to that beneficiary under the deed. Section 45-6-413 sets out the rest of the rules:

  • A beneficiary who does not survive the owner takes nothing, and that interest lapses.
  • Several beneficiaries take equal, undivided shares with no right of survivorship.
  • If one of several beneficiaries lapses, the others take that share in proportion to their interests.
  • If the owner was a joint owner who is survived by another joint owner, the property belongs to the survivor under the right of survivorship. The deed works only if the owner was the last surviving joint owner.
  • The beneficiary takes subject to all recorded conveyances, mortgages, liens and other recorded interests that exist at the owner's death.
  • The transfer is made without covenant or warranty of title, even if the deed says otherwise.

The court guide describes the beneficiary's practical step: file a copy of the death certificate with the county clerk where the real estate is located, after which title passes without probate.

sections.h2: Does the beneficiary owe the owner's debts?
sections.html:
Possibly, to a limited extent. Section 45-6-415 says a beneficiary of a transfer on death deed is liable for an allowed claim against the transferor's probate estate, and for statutory allowances to a surviving spouse and children, to the extent provided in 45-6-102 NMSA 1978.

The deed therefore avoids a probate filing for the house itself but does not make the house untouchable. A mortgage stays attached, and a beneficiary who plans to keep the property still has to keep up payments. Recorded liens also travel with the house, as 45-6-413 states.

The probate court rules say much the same from the estate side. They describe the probate estate as generally excluding property that passes automatically to a listed beneficiary, and they include land subject to transfer on death deeds in that group.

sections.h2: How do transfer on death deeds compare with other routes?
sections.html:
The right route depends on what the owner wants to control. The table summarizes what the sources say for each.

RouteWhat the source saysSource
Transfer on death deedRecorded before death; revocable by recorded instrument; beneficiary gets no interest during the owner's life45-6-409, 45-6-411, 45-6-412
ProbateMay be filed in the probate court of the county where the person lived, between 5 days and 3 years after death; filing cost $30NM Courts self-help guide
Small estate affidavitApplies to estates under $50,000 without real property, after 30 days if no probate is openNM Courts self-help guide
Personal representative's deedMay be needed to move real property out of the decedent's name when the estate includes itNM Courts self-help guide

The self-help guide at selfrepresentation.nmcourts.gov explains probate steps in plain language, and the statute text for 45-6-413 is short enough to read in full.

sections.h2: What if you want to sell a house that has a transfer on death deed?
sections.html:
The answer depends on whether the owner is alive. An owner who is alive can sell as usual, because the deed does not limit the right to transfer. A sale closes with the owner's own signature. Once the owner no longer holds the property at death, the deed has nothing left to transfer.

After an owner dies, the beneficiary has to establish ownership of record first by filing the death certificate with the county clerk. Selling comes next. A buyer will see the recorded deed, the death certificate and any recorded liens in the chain of title. Because the deed passes the house without warranty, the beneficiary should expect the buyer to review the title closely.

Inherited houses often come with repairs, back taxes or relatives who live far away. A cash sale can shorten the process, but it does not change the rules above. Cash Home Buyers makes no price promises in advance, and the beneficiary should confirm title steps with an attorney or title company before signing a contract.

faqs.q: Does a New Mexico transfer on death deed avoid probate?
faqs.a: For the house itself, yes, according to the New Mexico Courts guide: the beneficiary files a copy of the death certificate with the county clerk and title passes without probate. The beneficiary can still be liable for allowed claims against the probate estate under 45-6-415.

faqs.q: Must the deed be recorded before the owner dies?
faqs.a: Yes. Section 45-6-409 requires recording before the transferor's death in the office of the county clerk where the property is located.

faqs.q: Does the beneficiary have to be told about the deed?
faqs.a: No. Section 45-6-410 says no notice, delivery or acceptance by the beneficiary is needed during the owner's life, and no consideration is required.

faqs.q: Can the owner sell the house after signing a transfer on death deed?
faqs.a: Yes. Under 45-6-412 the deed does not affect the owner's right to transfer or encumber the property, and the beneficiary has no legal or equitable interest while the owner is alive.

faqs.q: What happens if the beneficiary dies before the owner?
faqs.a: The beneficiary's interest lapses under 45-6-413. If there were several beneficiaries, the surviving ones take the lapsed share in proportion to their interests.

faqs.q: Does a transfer on death deed come with a warranty of title?
faqs.a: No. Section 45-6-413 says the deed transfers property without covenant or warranty of title, even if the deed contains a contrary provision.
